Air traffic control calamity disrupting hundreds of US flights spotlights the aging system
The same Philadelphia facility that had the radar outages in the spring of 2025 lost both its primary and backup data lines at the same time on Monday.
Communications failures that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast on Monday have put the spotlight back on the aging systems that air traffic controllers rely on in the U.S.
Congress already handed the Federal Aviation Administration $12.5 billion last year to overhaul technology after the deadliest U.S. plane crash in more than two decades killed 67 people when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River and a series of radar outages later that spring led to widespread cancellations at Newark Liberty International Airport.
The same Philadelphia facility that had the radar outages in the spring of 2025 lost both its primary and backup data lines at the same time on Monday. But that regional air traffic control center isn’t alone; similar communications outages have also disrupted flights in Minneapolis and Dallas over the past year.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy quickly turned Monday’s disruption that hit every major airport in the New York area into the latest example of why he’s asking Congress for $20 billion more to pay for the next phase of the air traffic control overhaul. Airlines were working to recover from the outage on Tuesday, but FlightAware.com showed nearly 100 flights had been canceled by midday because a number of planes and crews were out of position after Monday’s cancellations.
“I have money for some of the telecom replacing old copper wires. Bringing in new fiber so it’s faster. The problem is this is a 40-year-old architecture or design,” Duffy said on Fox News Tuesday. “I need new money to do a whole new design — a new architecture of telecom so it will never go down.”
The aviation industry’s Modern Skies Coalition backed Duffy’s plan again and urged Congress to approve the money because the latest disruptions “demonstrate how critical it is to replace the antiquated technology and outdated systems that underpin our nation’s air traffic control infrastructure.”
Both the primary and backup lines failed on Monday
A switch on the primary communications line at the regional FAA air traffic control facility in Philadelphia failed Monday morning, but when it turned to the backup fiber optic line authorities discovered that it had been inadvertently severed by railroad construction workers. The failures left controllers without radar or communications for hours. The switch is part of the equipment scheduled to be replaced.
The outage brought commercial air traffic to a near-standstill at Newark for much of the day, with no commercial flights landing at the airport from about 9:40 a.m. to just after 5:20 p.m. local time, according to flight tracking site Flightradar24.
More than 200 flights into and out of Philadelphia International Airport were also canceled, while disruptions hit LaGuardia and Kennedy airports in New York. Flights had resumed by Monday evening.
Technical problems that affect Newark Liberty Airport tend to get outsized attention because it’s a key hub for United Airlines. During the spring of 2025, controllers in Philadelphia briefly lost radar several times and then staffing shortages at the facility prompted the FAA to restrict traffic.
The Dallas outage last September disrupted American Airlines’ key hub, and last month’s communications failure at a regional air traffic control facility in Minneapolis halted flights across several Midwestern states and led to numerous diversions and delays.
Problems at key regional control facilities affect flights nationwide
Sheldon Jacobson, whose research contributed to the design of the TSA PreCheck system, said the FAA needs to make sure that its backup systems are independent of the primary line to reduce the chance that both will fail at the same time. And he said maybe the agency should look at adding a third line to have an additional backup system.
“When any one of these systems goes down, it doesn’t just affect that airport. Because these are major hubs, it affects literally dozens of other airports and literally thousands of passengers,” said Jacobson, who is an engineering professor at the University of Illinois.
The National Air Traffic Controllers Association said the controllers who were on duty Monday did an exceptional job making sure everyone remained safe even when they lost their radios and radar.
“No controller starts their shift with the expectation that the equipment will fail them, but when it does they display professionalism and skill,” the union said in a statement.
Ongoing upgrades can help make the system more reliable
The FAA says it has already replaced 3,346 communications lines and 190 voice switches across the country since the agency received what Duffy called a $12.5 billion down payment on the overhaul. But the plan also calls for redesigning the computer system that air traffic controllers rely on, shifting computing online to the cloud and adding a new AI-based system to help predict problems. Duffy says he doesn’t have enough money for those projects yet.
Robert Poole, who leads transportation research at the Reason Foundation think tank he founded in the late 1970s, said the FAA needs reliable long-term funding to complete all the needed upgrades, and that is hard to get from Congress. He has long argued for spinning off air traffic control from the FAA and creating an independent agency that would be funded by ticket fees the airlines charge.
“We know what kind of technology is really needed to do that, but you can’t do that on drips and drabs of annual appropriations,” Poole said.

By Rajwa Quasim
Airports across the northeastern U.S. resumed operations Monday after a telecommunications failure at a Federal Aviation Administration radar facility disrupted flights across the region for hours.
The outage affected major airports in the New York and Philadelphia areas, including Newark Liberty, Teterboro, Philadelphia International, LaGuardia and John F. Kennedy International. While communications have been restored, airlines continued working through delays and cancellations caused by the disruption.
The FAA said the primary telecommunications circuit at its Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control Facility (TRACON) failed earlier Monday. The facility typically handles air traffic across a large area around Philadelphia and New York, managing flights in and around some of the region’s busiest airports.

The situation was further complicated when the backup fiber system was also found to be unavailable because of a break in the line.
A fiber optic line in New Jersey that was supposed to serve as a backup was accidentally damaged during construction work near an Amtrak rail line, affecting Verizon communications lines. Verizon said contractors working in the area dug up and cut the cable and that the damage was not caused by the telecommunications company. The company added that its cables had been properly placed.
Newark was among the airports hardest hit by the disruption. According to flight-tracking data, about 107 flights had been diverted from Newark to 34 different airports by 5:30 p.m. local time. Washington Dulles International Airport received 19 of the diverted flights. More than 300 flights had been canceled as of Monday evening.
The timing of the incident also created additional pressure for New York. The city is hosting the 81st United Nations General Assembly this week, bringing leaders and diplomats from around the world. The disruption affected some high-profile travelers, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. His office said his arrival was delayed, causing him to miss a scheduled meeting.

The incident has raised renewed questions about the country’s air traffic control infrastructure. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency aims to replace the existing system with a modern federal enterprise network. He said, “This is why we’re asking for budget to replace all of this stuff … We’re pulling copper up and putting fiber down, but it’s the same data architecture that we’ve had for 50 years.”
“This incident underscores the need for additional funding to modernize aging infrastructure and prevent disruptions like this in the future,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in an X post. He added, “This is not a new problem. It’s an old system that we were stuck working with.”
The Philadelphia TRACON facility has faced similar problems in the past. In 2025, a brief outage contributed to flight disruptions around Newark.
Duffy announced plans last year for a “brand new air traffic control system” by 2028, making modernization a key priority of his tenure. He said more than 4,600 sites would receive new high-speed network connections, replacing outdated telecommunications lines with fiber, wireless and satellite links by 2028.
The latest incident has renewed calls to strengthen the communications infrastructure and ensure reliable backup systems are in place to prevent similar disruptions in the future.

Disney World travelers on September 21, 2026, were left stranded after a widespread outage grounded hundreds of flights. Here’s what we know about this Northeast technical outage.
Disney World Trips Halted Thanks to Widespread Outage
Flights were moving again through New York City-area airports Tuesday, September 22, but the fallout from Monday’s air traffic control communications failure had not disappeared. Delays and cancellations remained after damaged communications lines tied to the Federal Aviation Administration’s Philadelphia facility disrupted Newark Liberty International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, LaGuardia Airport and other Northeast airports.
For Walt Disney World travelers, the disruption created an expensive travel problem: a vacation clock that keeps running even when the plane does not. Guests scheduled to fly from the Northeast to Orlando could face late arrivals, missed first-day plans or canceled flights.
Northeast Flight Disruptions Continue After Communications Failure
The Associated Press reported that hundreds of flights were canceled Monday, including more than 600 into and out of Newark. More than 200 flights involving Philadelphia International Airport were also canceled, while LaGuardia and Kennedy were affected.
According to AP, the FAA facility’s primary communications line failed Monday, while a backup fiber-optic line had also been severed during railroad construction work. The combination left controllers without radar or communications for hours.
FAA records show equipment-related ground stops at Newark and Philadelphia. By late Monday, however, an FAA operations advisory said ground-delay programs for JFK, LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia had been canceled.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the telecommunications lines had been repaired and operations were resuming, while warning that clearing existing delays would take time. AP reported roughly 40 delays and nearly 60 cancellations at Newark early Tuesday.
Disney World Vacations Can Lose Hours Before Guests Reach Florida
The outage did not close Walt Disney World, and there is no confirmed indication that Magic Kingdom, EPCOT, Disney’s Hollywood Studios or Disney’s Animal Kingdom changed operations because of it. The direct problem for Disney vacationers was transportation: affected travelers could not reach Central Florida on their original schedule.
Inside the Magic has previously covered how Orlando International Airport delays can threaten theme-park access and cascade into later baggage pickup, ground transportation and hotel check-in.
A family planning to land at MCO in the afternoon may have dining, Lightning Lane or evening park plans built around that arrival. A cancellation can erase that schedule, while a lengthy delay can compress a planned Disney day into only a few usable hours.
The disruption also lands in a year when MCO remains a major Disney gateway. Inside the Magic reported on Orlando International Airport’s passenger growth, including its climb to seventh among North American airports in 2025 passenger traffic.
A Stranded Traveler Still Has Disney Reservations Waiting
An airline cancellation does not automatically reorganize the rest of a vacation. Disney hotel nights, park plans, dining reservations and transportation arrangements exist on separate systems and may carry their own modification or cancellation terms.
Travelers should therefore treat a disrupted flight as an itinerary problem, not simply an airport problem. Check the airline first, then review time-sensitive Disney plans in My Disney Experience and contact the relevant provider when a delay threatens a reservation.
Inside the Magic’s coverage of an Orlando airport blackout showed how airport failures can spill into Disney travel days. A recent MCO weather disruption similarly illustrated how individual travelers can remain affected even after broader operating conditions improve.
Guests should not assume resumed operations mean every itinerary is normal. The FAA advises travelers to obtain flight-specific delay information from their air carrier.
Newark’s Problems Exposed a Larger Air-Traffic Weak Point
Monday’s failure was especially significant at Newark. AP reported that commercial traffic came to a near-standstill for much of the day, with no commercial arrivals from about 9:40 a.m. until shortly after 5:20 p.m.
The Philadelphia facility has also been central to earlier Newark reliability concerns. In a prior statement, the FAA detailed Newark telecommunications improvements and said telecommunications lines carry radar data from New York to the Philadelphia TRACON, where controllers handle Newark arrivals and departures. The agency had outlined additional high-bandwidth connections, upgraded fiber-optic technology and other redundancy work.
Monday showed why that infrastructure matters beyond the airports immediately involved. Reuters reported that roughly 7,000 flights were delayed or canceled during the disruption and more than 100 flights were diverted. A Northeast failure can propagate through aircraft rotations, crews and connecting itineraries across the national network.
For Disney travelers, that means a flight does not need to originate at Newark to become entangled in the recovery.
What Disney World Travelers Should Watch Next
Operations had resumed by Tuesday, but residual delays and cancellations remained. Travelers scheduled through Newark, JFK, LaGuardia, Philadelphia or connecting airports should verify their flight before leaving for the airport rather than relying solely on news that the communications lines are repaired.
Inside the Magic has also tracked major 2026 changes at Orlando International Airport and Disney’s evolving airport luggage-transfer options, useful context for guests rebuilding an arrival or departure plan.
What remains unknown is how long individual airline schedules will take to fully normalize and exactly how many Walt Disney World-bound passengers were affected; no verified Disney-specific passenger count has been released. Walt Disney World has not announced an operational closure tied to the Northeast outage.
The infrastructure failure is repaired. For guests whose Disney vacation was pushed off schedule, the practical recovery ends only when their replacement flight reaches Orlando.
